statement.p: Use the Divergence Theorem to calculate the flux of the vector fields \vec F_1 = -5z\vec i + 5x\vec k and \vec F_2 = -5z\vec i + (5-5y)\vec j + 5x\vec k through the surface S given by the sphere of radius a centered at the origin with outwards orientation. Be sure that you are able to explain your answers geometrically.
With W giving the interior of the sphere,

static.solution:
\mbox{div } \vec F_1 = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-5z) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(0) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(5x) = 0. and \mbox{div } \vec F_2 = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(-5z) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(5-5y) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(5x) = -5. Hence, \int_S\vec F_1\cdot d\vec A = \int_W 0\,dV = 0, and \int_S\vec F_2\cdot d\vec A = \int_W -5\,dV = -5\int_W\,dV = \frac{-20\pi a^3}{3}.
This makes sense, because, the vector field \vec F_1 is flowing around the y-axis and is therefore always tangent to the sphere, so that the flux is always zero. \vec F_2, however, adds a component in the y direction that points in for y>0 and out (for sufficiently large negative y) for y\lt 0, and therefore results in a non-zero flux.
